question: Which data structure follows the Last In First Out (LIFO) principle?
option_b: Stack
correct_answer: Stack
explanation: A stack removes the most recently added element first — this is the LIFO property.

question: In a singly linked list each node contains data and what else?
option_a: A pointer to the previous node
option_b: A pointer to the next node
option_c: The total size of the list
correct_answer: A pointer to the next node
explanation: Each node in a singly linked list stores data and a reference (pointer) to the next node in the sequence.

question: What is the maximum number of children a node can have in a binary tree?
explanation: By definition a binary tree node has at most two children: a left child and a right child.

question: Which data structure uses First In First Out (FIFO) ordering?
option_b: Queue
correct_answer: Queue
explanation: A queue processes elements in the order they were added — the first element enqueued is the first dequeued.

question: What does a hash table use to map keys to array indices?
option_b: Hash function
correct_answer: Hash function
explanation: A hash function computes an index from the key so the value can be stored and retrieved in near-constant time.

question: Which traversal visits the root node before its subtrees?
option_b: Post-order
correct_answer: Pre-order
explanation: Pre-order traversal visits the root first then recursively visits the left subtree followed by the right subtree.

question: What is the time complexity of accessing an element by index in an array?
option_b: O(log n)
explanation: Arrays support constant-time random access because elements are stored in contiguous memory locations.

question: What is the worst-case time complexity of inserting into a hash table with chaining?
option_b: O(log n)
correct_answer: O(n)
explanation: If all keys hash to the same bucket the chain becomes a linked list of length n so insertion degrades to O(n).

question: Which self-balancing BST guarantees O(log n) height by enforcing a color invariant on every node?
option_b: AVL Tree
correct_answer: Red-Black Tree
explanation: A Red-Black Tree colors every node red or black and enforces rules that keep the longest path at most twice the shortest guaranteeing O(log n) height.

question: In a min-heap which element is always at the root?
option_b: The median element
correct_answer: The smallest element
explanation: A min-heap maintains the heap property: every parent is less than or equal to its children so the minimum is always at the root.

question: What is the amortized time complexity of appending to a dynamic array that doubles in size when full?
option_b: O(log n)
explanation: Although individual resizes cost O(n) they happen rarely enough that the amortized cost per append is O(1).

question: Which data structure is best suited for implementing an LRU cache?
option_b: Stack
correct_answer: HashMap + Doubly Linked List
explanation: An LRU cache needs O(1) lookup (hash map) and O(1) insertion/removal of the least-recently-used item (doubly linked list).

question: What is the space complexity of storing a graph with V vertices and E edges using an adjacency list?
option_b: O(V + E)
correct_answer: O(V + E)
explanation: An adjacency list stores a list of neighbors for each vertex using O(V) vertex entries plus O(E) edge entries total.

question: After deleting the root of a max-heap how is the heap property restored?
option_b: Swap root with last element then heapify down
correct_answer: Swap root with last element then heapify down
explanation: The last element replaces the root then sift-down (heapify) swaps it with its larger child repeatedly until the max-heap property holds.

question: A Bloom filter may return false positives but never false negatives. Why is this the case?
option_b: It uses multiple hash functions mapping to a bit array
option_c: It uses a sorted array with binary search
option_d: It discards elements after a timeout
correct_answer: It uses multiple hash functions mapping to a bit array
explanation: A Bloom filter sets bits at multiple hash positions. A lookup checks all positions — an absent element may collide with bits set by other elements (false positive) but a present element always has all its bits set (no false negative).

question: What is the time complexity of building a binary heap from an unsorted array using the bottom-up method?
option_b: O(n²)
correct_answer: O(n)
explanation: Bottom-up heap construction calls heapify on each non-leaf node. The total work sums to O(n) because most nodes are near the bottom and require few swaps.

question: In a B-tree of minimum degree t what is the maximum number of keys a node can hold?
explanation: A B-tree node of minimum degree t can hold at most 2t − 1 keys and 2t children. This keeps the tree balanced and optimizes disk reads.

question: Which data structure supports union and find operations in nearly O(1) amortized time using path compression and union by rank?
option_b: Trie
correct_answer: Disjoint Set (Union-Find)
explanation: Union-Find with path compression and union by rank achieves an amortized time complexity of O(α(n)) per operation where α is the inverse Ackermann function — effectively constant.

question: What problem does a skip list solve compared to a standard sorted linked list?
option_b: O(log n) expected search time
correct_answer: O(log n) expected search time
explanation: A skip list adds multiple levels of forward pointers to a sorted linked list enabling binary-search-like behavior with O(log n) expected time for search insert and delete.

question: In a segment tree built over an array of n elements how many nodes does the tree contain in the worst case?
option_b: 2n
correct_answer: 4n
explanation: A segment tree is typically allocated as a complete binary tree. For n elements the array representation may need up to 4n nodes to handle non-power-of-two sizes safely.

question: What is the key advantage of a Fibonacci heap over a binary heap for Dijkstra's algorithm?
option_b: O(1) amortized decrease-key
correct_answer: O(1) amortized decrease-key
explanation: Fibonacci heaps support decrease-key in O(1) amortized time reducing Dijkstra's total complexity to O(V log V + E) compared to O((V+E) log V) with a binary heap.

question: What does Big-O notation describe about an algorithm?
option_a: The exact running time in seconds
option_b: An upper bound on growth rate as input size increases
correct_answer: An upper bound on growth rate as input size increases
explanation: Big-O gives an asymptotic upper bound on how an algorithm's time or space requirements grow relative to input size.

question: Which sorting algorithm repeatedly finds the minimum element and places it at the beginning?
option_b: Quick Sort
correct_answer: Selection Sort
explanation: Selection sort scans the unsorted portion for the minimum element and swaps it into the next sorted position on each pass.

question: What is the time complexity of linear search in the worst case?
option_b: O(log n)
correct_answer: O(n)
explanation: Linear search checks each element one by one — in the worst case the target is last or absent requiring n comparisons.

question: Binary search requires the input array to be in what state?
option_b: Sorted
correct_answer: Sorted
explanation: Binary search halves the search space at each step which only works correctly when the array is sorted.

question: Which algorithm technique solves a problem by breaking it into smaller subproblems solving each recursively and combining results?
option_b: Divide and Conquer
correct_answer: Divide and Conquer
explanation: Divide and conquer splits the problem into independent subproblems solves them recursively and merges the solutions.

question: What is the time complexity of Bubble Sort in the worst case?
option_b: O(n log n)
correct_answer: O(n²)
explanation: Bubble sort makes n passes through the array swapping adjacent elements — nested loops give O(n²) in the worst case.

question: Which search algorithm works by checking every element one by one from start to end?
option_b: Interpolation Search
correct_answer: Linear Search
explanation: Linear search iterates through the collection sequentially comparing each element with the target.

question: What is the average-case time complexity of Quick Sort?
option_b: O(n log n)
correct_answer: O(n log n)
explanation: Quick sort's average case partitions the array into roughly equal halves at each level of recursion giving O(n log n) comparisons.

question: Which algorithmic paradigm stores solutions to overlapping subproblems to avoid redundant computation?
option_b: Dynamic Programming
correct_answer: Dynamic Programming
explanation: Dynamic programming identifies overlapping subproblems and stores their results (memoization or tabulation) so each subproblem is solved only once.

question: In Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm why must all edge weights be non-negative?
option_b: The greedy choice assumes shorter partial paths remain shorter
option_d: The algorithm only works on trees
correct_answer: The greedy choice assumes shorter partial paths remain shorter
explanation: Dijkstra greedily finalizes the shortest known distance to a node. A negative edge could later provide a shorter path to an already-finalized node violating this greedy invariant.

question: What is the recurrence relation for Merge Sort?
explanation: Merge sort splits the array into two halves (2 subproblems of size n/2) and merges them in O(n) time.

question: Which graph traversal algorithm uses a queue and visits nodes level by level?
option_b: Breadth-First Search
correct_answer: Breadth-First Search
explanation: BFS uses a FIFO queue to explore all neighbors at the current depth before moving to the next level.

question: A greedy algorithm for the activity selection problem sorts activities by what criterion?
option_b: Duration
correct_answer: Finish time
explanation: Sorting by finish time and always picking the next compatible activity yields the maximum number of non-overlapping activities — a classic greedy strategy.

question: What is the worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort and when does it occur?
option_a: O(n log n) when the array is sorted
option_b: O(n²) when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element
option_c: O(n) when all elements are equal
option_d: O(n²) when the array is random
correct_answer: O(n²) when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element
explanation: If the pivot consistently produces maximally unbalanced partitions (e.g. already sorted array with first-element pivot) recursion depth reaches n and total work becomes O(n²).

question: What is the time complexity of the Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) string matching algorithm?
option_b: O(n + m)
correct_answer: O(n + m)
explanation: KMP preprocesses the pattern to build a failure function in O(m) then scans the text in O(n) — total O(n + m) without backtracking on the text.

question: Which problem is solved by finding a Hamiltonian cycle of minimum total weight in a complete graph?
option_b: Shortest Path
correct_answer: Travelling Salesman Problem
explanation: The TSP asks for the minimum-cost tour visiting every vertex exactly once and returning to the start — a Hamiltonian cycle of minimum weight.

question: What does the Master Theorem directly solve?
option_b: Recurrences of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)
correct_answer: Recurrences of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)
explanation: The Master Theorem applies to divide-and-conquer recurrences where the problem splits into a subproblems each of size n/b with combine cost f(n).

question: In the context of NP-completeness what does a polynomial-time reduction from problem A to problem B prove?
option_b: B is at least as hard as A
option_c: A and B have the same solution
option_d: B can be solved in polynomial time
correct_answer: B is at least as hard as A
explanation: If A ≤ₚ B then any polynomial-time algorithm for B would also solve A — so B is at least as hard as A.

question: Which algorithm finds the strongly connected components of a directed graph in O(V + E) time?
option_b: Tarjan's algorithm
correct_answer: Tarjan's algorithm
explanation: Tarjan's SCC algorithm uses a single DFS pass with a stack and low-link values to identify all strongly connected components in linear time.

question: What is the time complexity of the Floyd-Warshall all-pairs shortest path algorithm?
option_b: O(V² log V)
correct_answer: O(V³)
explanation: Floyd-Warshall uses three nested loops over V vertices to consider every intermediate vertex for every pair giving O(V³).

question: In a maximum-flow network what does the max-flow min-cut theorem state?
option_a: Maximum flow equals minimum edge weight
option_b: Maximum flow equals the capacity of the minimum cut
option_c: Maximum flow equals the number of paths
option_d: Flow is always equal to demand
correct_answer: Maximum flow equals the capacity of the minimum cut
explanation: The theorem proves that the value of the maximum flow from source to sink equals the total capacity of the edges in the minimum s-t cut.

question: What does SQL stand for?
option_b: Simple Query Logic
correct_answer: Structured Query Language
explanation: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for managing and querying relational databases.

question: Which SQL keyword is used to retrieve data from a database?
option_b: UPDATE
correct_answer: SELECT
explanation: The SELECT statement queries one or more tables and returns the matching rows as a result set.

question: A primary key in a relational database must be what?
option_b: Unique and not null
correct_answer: Unique and not null
explanation: A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table and by definition cannot contain NULL values.

question: Which type of database relationship links one record in table A to many records in table B?
option_b: One-to-Many
correct_answer: One-to-Many
explanation: A one-to-many relationship means a single row in table A can relate to multiple rows in table B — for example one department having many employees.

question: What does the WHERE clause do in a SQL query?
option_b: Filters rows based on a condition
correct_answer: Filters rows based on a condition
explanation: The WHERE clause specifies a condition that each row must satisfy to be included in the query results.

question: Which SQL command is used to add a new row to a table?
option_b: INSERT
correct_answer: INSERT
explanation: INSERT INTO adds a new row of data to an existing table.

question: What is a foreign key?
option_b: A column that references the primary key of another table
option_c: A unique identifier within the same table
correct_answer: A column that references the primary key of another table
explanation: A foreign key creates a link between two tables by referencing the primary key in the parent table enforcing referential integrity.

question: What is the purpose of database normalization?
option_b: To reduce data redundancy and improve integrity
correct_answer: To reduce data redundancy and improve integrity
explanation: Normalization organizes tables to minimize duplicate data and dependency anomalies — each fact is stored in exactly one place.

question: Which normal form eliminates transitive dependencies?
option_b: Second Normal Form (2NF)
correct_answer: Third Normal Form (3NF)
explanation: 3NF requires that every non-key attribute depends only on the primary key — not transitively through another non-key attribute.

question: What is the ACID property 'Atomicity' in database transactions?
option_a: All transactions run at the same time
option_b: A transaction is all-or-nothing
option_d: Transactions are isolated from each other
correct_answer: A transaction is all-or-nothing
explanation: Atomicity guarantees that either all operations in a transaction complete successfully or none of them take effect — partial execution is impossible.

question: Which type of SQL JOIN returns only the rows with matching values in both tables?
option_b: RIGHT JOIN
correct_answer: INNER JOIN
explanation: An INNER JOIN returns only those rows where the join condition is satisfied in both tables — unmatched rows are excluded.

question: What does a database index primarily improve?
option_b: Read query performance
correct_answer: Read query performance
explanation: An index creates a sorted data structure (like a B-tree) that lets the database locate rows much faster than scanning the entire table.

question: In a relational database what is a view?
option_a: A physical copy of a table
option_b: A virtual table defined by a stored query
correct_answer: A virtual table defined by a stored query
explanation: A view is a named SELECT query that behaves like a table but does not store data itself — it dynamically retrieves data when queried.

question: What is a deadlock in database systems?
option_a: A query that takes too long
option_b: Two transactions waiting for each other's locks indefinitely
correct_answer: Two transactions waiting for each other's locks indefinitely
explanation: A deadlock occurs when transaction A holds lock X and waits for lock Y while transaction B holds Y and waits for X — neither can proceed.

question: What is the difference between a clustered and a non-clustered index?
option_a: Clustered indexes are faster; non-clustered are slower
option_b: A clustered index determines physical row order; a non-clustered index uses a separate structure pointing to rows
option_c: Clustered indexes work on views; non-clustered indexes work on tables
correct_answer: A clustered index determines physical row order; a non-clustered index uses a separate structure pointing to rows
explanation: A clustered index sorts and stores table rows by the index key (one per table). A non-clustered index maintains a separate B-tree with pointers back to the data rows.

question: In the context of ACID what does the Isolation level 'Serializable' guarantee?
option_b: Transactions execute as if they were run one after another
correct_answer: Transactions execute as if they were run one after another
explanation: Serializable is the strictest isolation level — it ensures concurrent transactions produce the same result as some serial execution order preventing all anomalies.

question: What problem can occur at the 'Read Committed' isolation level but not at 'Repeatable Read'?
option_b: Non-repeatable reads
correct_answer: Non-repeatable reads
explanation: At Read Committed a transaction may see different values for the same row if another transaction commits between reads. Repeatable Read prevents this by locking read rows.

question: What is a write-ahead log (WAL) and why is it important?
option_a: A log written after transaction commit for auditing
option_b: A log written before changes are applied to disk ensuring crash recovery
correct_answer: A log written before changes are applied to disk ensuring crash recovery
explanation: WAL writes all modifications to a log file before applying them to data pages. After a crash the log can replay committed changes and undo uncommitted ones.

question: Which concurrency control protocol uses timestamps to order transactions without locks?
option_b: Timestamp Ordering Protocol
correct_answer: Timestamp Ordering Protocol
explanation: The timestamp ordering protocol assigns a unique timestamp to each transaction and ensures read/write operations follow timestamp order — aborting transactions that violate the order.

question: In query optimization what does a cost-based optimizer use to choose an execution plan?
option_a: The length of the SQL statement
option_b: Statistics about table sizes and index selectivity
option_c: The order of columns in the SELECT clause
correct_answer: Statistics about table sizes and index selectivity
explanation: A cost-based optimizer estimates the I/O and CPU cost of different plans using statistics like row counts histogram distributions and index cardinality to pick the cheapest plan.

question: What is the CAP theorem in distributed databases?
option_a: Consistency Availability and Performance can all be achieved
option_b: You can guarantee at most two of Consistency Availability and Partition tolerance simultaneously
option_d: CAP only applies to NoSQL databases
correct_answer: You can guarantee at most two of Consistency Availability and Partition tolerance simultaneously
explanation: The CAP theorem states that in the presence of a network partition a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability — it cannot guarantee all three.

question: What is the primary function of an operating system?
option_b: Manage hardware resources and provide services to applications
correct_answer: Manage hardware resources and provide services to applications
explanation: An OS acts as an intermediary between applications and hardware — managing CPU memory storage and I/O devices.

question: What is a process in an operating system?
option_b: A program in execution with its own memory and state
correct_answer: A program in execution with its own memory and state
explanation: A process is a running instance of a program including its code data stack program counter and allocated resources.

question: Which scheduling algorithm gives each process an equal time slice in round-robin fashion?
option_b: Shortest Job First
correct_answer: Round Robin
explanation: Round Robin assigns a fixed time quantum to each process cycling through the ready queue — ensuring fair CPU sharing.

question: What is virtual memory?
option_a: Memory on an external USB drive
option_b: A technique that uses disk space to extend available RAM
correct_answer: A technique that uses disk space to extend available RAM
explanation: Virtual memory maps address spaces to physical RAM and disk so programs can use more memory than physically available. The OS swaps pages between RAM and disk as needed.

question: What is the difference between a thread and a process?
option_b: A thread is a lightweight unit of execution within a process sharing its memory space
correct_answer: A thread is a lightweight unit of execution within a process sharing its memory space
explanation: Threads within the same process share code data and resources but each has its own stack and program counter. Processes have separate memory spaces.

question: What does the kernel of an operating system do?
option_b: Provides the core services including process scheduling and memory management
correct_answer: Provides the core services including process scheduling and memory management
explanation: The kernel is the core component of the OS — it manages CPU scheduling memory allocation device I/O and system calls.

question: What is a system call?
option_a: A phone call to tech support
option_b: An interface for user programs to request services from the OS kernel
correct_answer: An interface for user programs to request services from the OS kernel
explanation: System calls provide a controlled gateway for user-space programs to request kernel services like file I/O process creation and memory allocation.

question: What is a race condition?
option_a: When two programs compete for CPU time
option_b: When the outcome depends on the unpredictable order of thread execution
option_c: When a process runs too fast
correct_answer: When the outcome depends on the unpredictable order of thread execution
explanation: A race condition occurs when multiple threads access shared data concurrently and the result depends on the timing of their execution — leading to unpredictable behavior.

question: What is the purpose of a mutex (mutual exclusion lock)?
option_b: To ensure only one thread accesses a critical section at a time
correct_answer: To ensure only one thread accesses a critical section at a time
explanation: A mutex prevents concurrent access to a shared resource — a thread must acquire the lock before entering the critical section and release it when done.

question: Which page replacement algorithm is optimal but impractical to implement?
option_b: Least Recently Used (LRU)
correct_answer: Optimal (Bélády's)
explanation: The optimal algorithm replaces the page that will not be used for the longest time in the future. It requires future knowledge making it impractical but useful as a benchmark.

question: What is thrashing in the context of virtual memory?
option_b: Excessive page faults causing the system to spend more time swapping than executing
correct_answer: Excessive page faults causing the system to spend more time swapping than executing
explanation: Thrashing occurs when the working set of active pages exceeds available physical memory — the OS constantly swaps pages in and out and useful work drops dramatically.

question: What are the four necessary conditions for a deadlock to occur?
option_a: Mutual exclusion — hold and wait — no preemption — circular wait
option_b: Starvation — livelock — priority inversion — race condition
option_c: Mutual exclusion — FIFO — aging — round robin
correct_answer: Mutual exclusion — hold and wait — no preemption — circular wait
explanation: Coffman's conditions state that deadlock requires all four: mutual exclusion hold-and-wait no preemption and circular wait. Preventing any one condition prevents deadlock.

question: What is the difference between preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling?
option_b: In preemptive scheduling the OS can forcibly suspend a running process; in non-preemptive it cannot
option_c: Preemptive scheduling is only for I/O-bound processes
correct_answer: In preemptive scheduling the OS can forcibly suspend a running process; in non-preemptive it cannot
explanation: Preemptive schedulers can interrupt a running process (e.g. when its time quantum expires) while non-preemptive schedulers let each process run until it voluntarily yields or completes.

question: What is the purpose of a Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)?
option_b: To cache virtual-to-physical address translations for faster memory access
correct_answer: To cache virtual-to-physical address translations for faster memory access
explanation: The TLB is a hardware cache that stores recent page table entries. On a TLB hit the CPU skips the page table walk — dramatically speeding up memory access.

question: Explain the Banker's algorithm. What type of deadlock strategy does it implement?
option_b: Deadlock prevention
correct_answer: Deadlock avoidance
explanation: The Banker's algorithm is a deadlock avoidance strategy. Before granting a resource request it checks whether the system would remain in a safe state — if not the request is deferred.

question: What is priority inversion and how does priority inheritance solve it?
option_a: A high-priority process runs first; inheritance gives it more CPU
option_b: A low-priority task holding a lock blocks a high-priority task; priority inheritance temporarily raises the lock holder's priority
option_c: Priority is inverted when the scheduler fails; inheritance resets it
option_d: It only occurs in real-time systems and has no solution
correct_answer: A low-priority task holding a lock blocks a high-priority task; priority inheritance temporarily raises the lock holder's priority
explanation: Priority inversion occurs when a medium-priority task preempts a low-priority one that holds a lock needed by a high-priority task. Priority inheritance boosts the lock holder to prevent this.

question: What is the difference between internal and external fragmentation?
option_a: Internal wastes space inside allocated blocks; external wastes space between allocated blocks
option_b: Internal is on disk; external is in RAM
option_c: Internal is caused by paging; external is caused by segmentation only
correct_answer: Internal wastes space inside allocated blocks; external wastes space between allocated blocks
explanation: Internal fragmentation occurs when allocated memory exceeds what the process needs (e.g. fixed-size pages). External fragmentation occurs when free memory is scattered in small non-contiguous chunks.

question: How does Copy-on-Write (COW) optimize the fork() system call?
option_a: It copies the entire process memory immediately
option_b: It shares pages between parent and child and copies only when either writes to a page
option_c: It avoids creating a child process
option_d: It compresses the memory before copying
correct_answer: It shares pages between parent and child and copies only when either writes to a page
explanation: COW marks shared pages as read-only after fork(). A write triggers a page fault which copies just that page — avoiding the cost of duplicating the entire address space upfront.

question: What is the difference between a monolithic kernel and a microkernel?
option_b: A monolithic kernel runs all OS services in kernel space; a microkernel runs minimal services in kernel space and the rest in user space
option_c: Microkernels are faster because they have fewer features
correct_answer: A monolithic kernel runs all OS services in kernel space; a microkernel runs minimal services in kernel space and the rest in user space
explanation: Monolithic kernels (e.g. Linux) include drivers file systems and networking in kernel mode. Microkernels (e.g. Minix) keep only IPC scheduling and memory management in the kernel — other services run as user processes.

question: What is Bélády's anomaly in page replacement?
option_a: Adding more pages always reduces page faults
option_b: With FIFO replacement increasing the number of page frames can sometimes increase page faults
option_d: It means pages are loaded in the wrong order
correct_answer: With FIFO replacement increasing the number of page frames can sometimes increase page faults
explanation: Bélády's anomaly is counterintuitive: for FIFO page replacement certain reference strings cause more page faults with more frames. Stack-based algorithms like LRU never exhibit this anomaly.

question: In a real-time operating system what is the difference between hard and soft real-time constraints?
option_b: Hard real-time requires deadlines to be met absolutely; soft real-time allows occasional deadline misses
option_c: Soft real-time is only for multimedia
correct_answer: Hard real-time requires deadlines to be met absolutely; soft real-time allows occasional deadline misses
explanation: In hard real-time systems (e.g. aircraft control) missing a deadline is a system failure. Soft real-time (e.g. video streaming) tolerates occasional misses with degraded quality.

question: What does IP stand for in networking?
option_b: Internet Protocol
correct_answer: Internet Protocol
explanation: The Internet Protocol (IP) is responsible for addressing and routing packets across networks to their destination.

question: Which layer of the OSI model is responsible for end-to-end data transfer and error recovery?
option_b: Data Link
correct_answer: Transport
explanation: The Transport layer (Layer 4) provides reliable end-to-end communication through segmentation flow control and error recovery — e.g. TCP.

question: What is the purpose of DNS in networking?
option_b: To translate domain names into IP addresses
correct_answer: To translate domain names into IP addresses
explanation: The Domain Name System maps human-readable domain names (like google.com) to IP addresses so browsers can locate servers.

question: What is the difference between TCP and UDP?
option_b: TCP provides reliable ordered delivery while UDP is connectionless and faster but unreliable
option_c: UDP is used only for email
option_d: TCP does not use IP addresses
correct_answer: TCP provides reliable ordered delivery while UDP is connectionless and faster but unreliable
explanation: TCP ensures packets arrive in order with error checking and retransmission. UDP sends packets without guarantees — useful for real-time applications like video calls.

question: What does a router do in a computer network?
option_b: Forwards data packets between different networks based on IP addresses
correct_answer: Forwards data packets between different networks based on IP addresses
explanation: A router examines the destination IP of each packet and forwards it toward its destination using routing tables.

question: What is a MAC address?
option_b: A unique hardware identifier assigned to a network interface card
option_d: The same as an IP address
correct_answer: A unique hardware identifier assigned to a network interface card
explanation: A MAC (Media Access Control) address is a 48-bit hardware address burned into a NIC — used for communication within a local network segment.

question: What is a subnet mask used for?
option_b: To determine which portion of an IP address identifies the network vs. the host
correct_answer: To determine which portion of an IP address identifies the network vs. the host
explanation: A subnet mask separates the network prefix from the host portion of an IP address allowing routers to determine if a destination is local or remote.

question: What is the three-way handshake in TCP?
option_b: The SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK sequence used to establish a TCP connection
option_c: A way to terminate a connection
correct_answer: The SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK sequence used to establish a TCP connection
explanation: The client sends SYN the server replies with SYN-ACK and the client confirms with ACK. This establishes a reliable connection before data transfer begins.

question: What is the purpose of ARP (Address Resolution Protocol)?
option_b: To resolve an IP address to a MAC address on a local network
option_d: To route packets across the internet
correct_answer: To resolve an IP address to a MAC address on a local network
explanation: When a host knows the destination IP but needs the MAC address for the local link it broadcasts an ARP request. The target replies with its MAC address.

question: What is NAT (Network Address Translation) used for?
option_b: To allow multiple devices on a private network to share a single public IP address
correct_answer: To allow multiple devices on a private network to share a single public IP address
explanation: NAT translates private IP addresses to a public IP for outgoing traffic and maps responses back — enabling many devices to access the internet through one public address.

question: What is the difference between a hub and a switch?
option_b: A hub broadcasts to all ports while a switch forwards frames only to the destination port
option_c: A switch is wireless and a hub is wired
correct_answer: A hub broadcasts to all ports while a switch forwards frames only to the destination port
explanation: A hub is a simple repeater that sends incoming frames to every port. A switch learns MAC addresses and forwards frames only to the correct port — reducing collisions.

question: What is CIDR notation and why is it used?
option_b: A compact representation of IP address ranges (e.g. 192.168.1.0/24) that enables flexible subnetting
correct_answer: A compact representation of IP address ranges (e.g. 192.168.1.0/24) that enables flexible subnetting
explanation: CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) replaces the rigid Class A/B/C system allowing networks to be subdivided into subnets of any size by specifying the prefix length.

question: How does DHCP assign IP addresses to devices on a network?
option_b: Through a Discover-Offer-Request-Acknowledge (DORA) process
option_c: By reading the device's MAC address only
correct_answer: Through a Discover-Offer-Request-Acknowledge (DORA) process
explanation: A DHCP client broadcasts a Discover message. The server responds with an Offer. The client sends a Request and the server confirms with an Acknowledge — dynamically assigning an IP.

question: What does a firewall do?
option_b: Monitors and filters incoming and outgoing network traffic based on security rules
correct_answer: Monitors and filters incoming and outgoing network traffic based on security rules
explanation: A firewall inspects packets against a set of rules and decides whether to allow or block traffic — protecting networks from unauthorized access and attacks.

question: How does TCP handle congestion control?
option_b: Through algorithms like Slow Start and Congestion Avoidance that dynamically adjust the sending rate
correct_answer: Through algorithms like Slow Start and Congestion Avoidance that dynamically adjust the sending rate
explanation: TCP starts with a small congestion window (slow start) doubling it each RTT until loss occurs. Then it switches to congestion avoidance (additive increase) and halves the window on loss (multiplicative decrease).

question: What is the difference between distance-vector and link-state routing protocols?
option_b: Distance-vector routers share routing tables with neighbors; link-state routers flood topology information to all routers
correct_answer: Distance-vector routers share routing tables with neighbors; link-state routers flood topology information to all routers
explanation: Distance-vector protocols (e.g. RIP) exchange distance tables with direct neighbors. Link-state protocols (e.g. OSPF) flood link-state advertisements so every router builds a complete topology map and runs Dijkstra.

question: What is BGP and why is it called the 'protocol of the internet'?
option_b: The Border Gateway Protocol — it manages routing between autonomous systems that make up the internet
correct_answer: The Border Gateway Protocol — it manages routing between autonomous systems that make up the internet
explanation: BGP is the exterior gateway protocol that enables autonomous systems (ISPs and large networks) to exchange reachability information — forming the global internet routing table.

question: How does TLS (Transport Layer Security) establish a secure connection?
option_b: Through a handshake that negotiates cipher suites exchanges certificates and derives session keys
option_d: By using UDP instead of TCP
correct_answer: Through a handshake that negotiates cipher suites exchanges certificates and derives session keys
explanation: The TLS handshake includes: client hello → server hello + certificate → key exchange → session key derivation. This establishes an encrypted channel before application data flows.

question: What is the count-to-infinity problem in distance-vector routing?
option_b: After a link failure routers slowly increment distance metrics through update loops before converging
correct_answer: After a link failure routers slowly increment distance metrics through update loops before converging
explanation: When a link fails distance-vector protocols can enter a loop where routers keep incrementing the cost metric — converging very slowly. Solutions include split horizon and poison reverse.

question: What is the purpose of the sliding window protocol in TCP?
option_b: To allow the sender to transmit multiple segments before requiring an acknowledgment improving throughput
correct_answer: To allow the sender to transmit multiple segments before requiring an acknowledgment improving throughput
explanation: The sliding window allows multiple unacknowledged segments to be in flight. The window size adjusts based on receiver capacity (flow control) and network conditions (congestion control).

question: How does an ARP spoofing attack work and what is its impact?
option_a: It floods the network with DNS requests
option_b: An attacker sends fake ARP replies to associate their MAC with a victim's IP enabling man-in-the-middle attacks
correct_answer: An attacker sends fake ARP replies to associate their MAC with a victim's IP enabling man-in-the-middle attacks
explanation: ARP has no authentication. An attacker can send unsolicited ARP replies mapping a legitimate IP to their own MAC — intercepting traffic intended for that IP.

question: What is encapsulation in object-oriented programming?
option_b: Bundling data and methods that operate on that data into a single unit (class) and restricting direct access
correct_answer: Bundling data and methods that operate on that data into a single unit (class) and restricting direct access
explanation: Encapsulation hides internal state behind methods — external code interacts through a public interface without knowing the implementation details.

question: What is inheritance in OOP?
option_b: A mechanism where a new class derives properties and behavior from an existing class
correct_answer: A mechanism where a new class derives properties and behavior from an existing class
explanation: Inheritance allows a child class to reuse and extend the functionality of a parent class — promoting code reuse and hierarchical design.

question: What is polymorphism?
option_b: The ability of different classes to be treated through the same interface while behaving differently
correct_answer: The ability of different classes to be treated through the same interface while behaving differently
explanation: Polymorphism lets a method call behave differently depending on the object's actual type — e.g. calling draw() on a Circle vs. a Rectangle produces different results.

question: What is a class in OOP?
option_b: A blueprint for creating objects that defines attributes and methods
correct_answer: A blueprint for creating objects that defines attributes and methods
explanation: A class defines the structure (attributes) and behavior (methods) that its instances (objects) will have.

question: What is the difference between a class and an object?
option_b: A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance of that class
correct_answer: A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance of that class
explanation: A class defines the template. An object is a concrete instance created from that class with its own attribute values stored in memory.

question: What is a constructor?
option_b: A special method called automatically when an object is created to initialize its state
correct_answer: A special method called automatically when an object is created to initialize its state
explanation: A constructor initializes the object's attributes when it is instantiated — e.g. __init__ in Python or the class-named method in Java/C++.

question: What does the 'this' (or 'self') keyword refer to in a method?
option_b: The current instance of the class on which the method is called
correct_answer: The current instance of the class on which the method is called
explanation: 'this' (Java/C++) or 'self' (Python) refers to the specific object invoking the method — allowing access to its own attributes and other methods.

question: What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding?
option_b: Overloading defines multiple methods with the same name but different parameters in the same class; overriding redefines a parent method in a child class
option_d: Overriding requires a new class name
correct_answer: Overloading defines multiple methods with the same name but different parameters in the same class; overriding redefines a parent method in a child class
explanation: Overloading is compile-time polymorphism (same method name different signatures). Overriding is runtime polymorphism (child replaces parent's method with its own implementation).

question: What is an abstract class?
option_b: A class that cannot be instantiated and may contain abstract methods that subclasses must implement
option_c: A class that is automatically deleted
correct_answer: A class that cannot be instantiated and may contain abstract methods that subclasses must implement
explanation: Abstract classes define a contract — they can have both implemented and abstract (unimplemented) methods. Subclasses must provide implementations for the abstract methods.

question: What is the difference between an interface and an abstract class?
option_b: An interface declares method signatures without implementation (prior to Java 8); an abstract class can include both implemented and abstract methods
correct_answer: An interface declares method signatures without implementation (prior to Java 8); an abstract class can include both implemented and abstract methods
explanation: Interfaces define a pure contract. Abstract classes can share common code. A class can implement multiple interfaces but typically extends only one abstract class.

question: What is the SOLID principle 'Single Responsibility'?
option_a: A class should have only one method
option_b: A class should have only one reason to change
option_c: A variable should hold only one value
option_d: A function should have only one parameter
correct_answer: A class should have only one reason to change
explanation: The Single Responsibility Principle states each class should be responsible for one aspect of functionality — reducing coupling and making changes localized.

question: What is composition in OOP and how does it differ from inheritance?
option_a: Composition is the same as inheritance
option_b: Composition builds complex objects by containing instances of other classes rather than inheriting from them
correct_answer: Composition builds complex objects by containing instances of other classes rather than inheriting from them
explanation: Composition uses a 'has-a' relationship (a Car has an Engine) while inheritance uses an 'is-a' relationship (a Dog is an Animal). Composition is generally more flexible.

question: What is the purpose of access modifiers like public private and protected?
option_b: To control the visibility and accessibility of class members
correct_answer: To control the visibility and accessibility of class members
explanation: Access modifiers enforce encapsulation: private restricts access to the class itself protected adds access for subclasses and public allows access from anywhere.

question: What is a design pattern in OOP?
option_b: A reusable solution template for a commonly occurring software design problem
correct_answer: A reusable solution template for a commonly occurring software design problem
explanation: Design patterns (like Singleton Factory Observer) provide proven approaches to recurring design challenges — they are not code but templates for how to structure solutions.

question: What is the Liskov Substitution Principle and why does violating it cause bugs?
option_a: Subclasses should always override all parent methods
option_b: Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of a subclass without altering program correctness
option_c: It requires all classes to be abstract
correct_answer: Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of a subclass without altering program correctness
explanation: LSP means subclasses must honor the contract of their parent. Violating it (e.g. a Square subclass of Rectangle that breaks setWidth/setHeight expectations) causes subtle bugs when code uses the parent type.

question: What problem does the Dependency Inversion Principle solve?
option_b: High-level modules depending on low-level implementation details making the system rigid
correct_answer: High-level modules depending on low-level implementation details making the system rigid
explanation: DIP states that high-level modules should depend on abstractions not concretions. This allows swapping implementations (e.g. switching databases) without modifying business logic.

question: How does the Observer pattern work and when should it be used?
option_b: Subjects maintain a list of observers and notify them of state changes — useful for event-driven architectures
correct_answer: Subjects maintain a list of observers and notify them of state changes — useful for event-driven architectures
explanation: The Observer pattern decouples event producers from consumers. When the subject's state changes all registered observers are automatically notified — used in GUIs event systems and reactive programming.

question: What is the diamond problem in multiple inheritance and how do languages solve it?
option_b: Ambiguity when a class inherits from two classes that share a common ancestor — solved by virtual inheritance or interfaces
correct_answer: Ambiguity when a class inherits from two classes that share a common ancestor — solved by virtual inheritance or interfaces
explanation: If class D inherits from B and C which both inherit from A then D has two copies of A's members. C++ uses virtual inheritance; Java/C# avoid the problem by allowing only single class inheritance with multiple interfaces.

question: What is the difference between shallow copy and deep copy of an object?
option_b: A shallow copy duplicates the object but shares references to nested objects; a deep copy recursively duplicates all nested objects
correct_answer: A shallow copy duplicates the object but shares references to nested objects; a deep copy recursively duplicates all nested objects
explanation: With a shallow copy modifying a nested object in the copy also affects the original. Deep copy creates fully independent copies at all levels — important for mutable nested structures.

question: How does the Strategy pattern differ from the Template Method pattern?
option_b: Strategy uses composition to swap entire algorithms at runtime; Template Method uses inheritance to let subclasses override specific steps
correct_answer: Strategy uses composition to swap entire algorithms at runtime; Template Method uses inheritance to let subclasses override specific steps
explanation: Strategy encapsulates algorithms as interchangeable objects (composition). Template Method defines a skeleton algorithm in a base class with hook methods that subclasses override (inheritance).

question: What is type erasure in Java generics and what are its implications?
option_a: Generics are erased at compile time
option_b: Generic type information is removed at runtime by the compiler — preventing runtime type checks on generic parameters
option_c: Generics are always preserved at runtime
option_d: Type erasure only affects primitive types
correct_answer: Generic type information is removed at runtime by the compiler — preventing runtime type checks on generic parameters
explanation: Java compiles generics by replacing type parameters with their bounds (usually Object) and inserting casts. This means you cannot do instanceof on generic types or create generic arrays at runtime.
